A service like DeleteMe can give you back some of that ownership. They file removal requests with hundreds of brokers on your behalf and keep at it when your data reappears.

The fix Varian predicted: when bargaining is costly, hire an agent. Songwriters use collecting societies; you can use a removal service.
The twist: he imagined you'd get paid for your data. Instead, you pay to claw it back. First grabber keeps the entitlement.

So a market grew in the gap: data brokers scrape your name, address, and old hotmail account, then sell it to anyone with a credit card.
Notice who's missing from that transaction: YOU. Nobody asks, pays, or consults you. The result? 4 billion robocalls a month.

In theory: you should own your data like a songwriter owns a song. Spotify needs a license to stream it, a dog food ad needs a separate one.
In practice: transaction costs kill this. You can't negotiate with 10,000 data brokers. Nobody pays enough to make it worth your morning.

What to make of Michigan

Abdul El-Sayed’s apparent victory is a big win for the left — but a disaster for polling and a case study in poor expectations management.
natesilver.net

Right, if he wins by any margin, it's still very impressive in an objective, non-expectations-adjusted sense.

It was also stupid AF for him to release a bunch of internals showing himself +13 or whatever.

If I were a campaign manager, not only would I never release internal polls, I'd also set a clear expectation that my campaign would never discuss polls, on or off the record. Voters couldn't give a shit, and the expectations management stuff often comes back to bite you.

A lot of the pollsters in Michigan are herdy and/or shitty. But it's a legit hard race to poll. Black voters, especially working-class Black voters, can be hard to reach. Young voters may be underrepresented in traditional surveys, but now we've mostly shifted to online panels.

And then you have some potential effects from non-response bias. AES supporters are almost certainly more enthusiastic than "Shy Stevens" voters, which can help with turnout, but it also means they might be more likely to respond to surveys, creating bias.

Then there's a question of what pollsters do with Arab-American voters. Important in Michigan, but still too small in an n=600 survey to be a reliable crosstab on their own. Do pollsters lump them in with "other"? With "white" (as the Census Bureau did prior to 2020.) Or what?

The implied projection from prediction markets is El-Sayed eventually winning by ~4, though a larger win or a Stevens win remain possible.

That would reflect a pretty big polling error, though I doubt AES will care so long as he wins.

To get a little meta here, a narrow El-Sayed win would be in the maximal "second-guessing zone" where the establishment will question whether it could have won if it had done X or Y differently, as opposed to being like "yeah, we suck". But that's getting ahead of ourselves.
